headline: Top scorer on a South Korean exam admits AI cheating

sources.title: 160 questions, only one wrong: top scorer in South Korea tax exam admits AI cheating (The Guardian)
South Korea's top scorer in tax accountancy exam admits cheating (BBC News)
Mini camera, AI and smartphone: How tax exam top scorer says he cheated under two proctors' noses (The Korea Herald)
PM vows to mobilize all national capabilities to prevent AI cheating on college entrance exam (The Korea Herald)

chunks.text: On Sunday, November 15, 2026, a man in South Korea {{owned up to}} cheating on a national exam with AI. The exam is for people who want to become [[tax accountants]], experts who help people with their taxes. The 34-year-old was the [[top scorer]] in both rounds, in April and July. His results had {{stood out}} for months. In the [[first round]], he got 159 of 160 questions right.

verbs.correct: To admit that you did something wrong
verbs.wrong: To ask another person to take a test
verbs.why: Kids often own up to small mistakes when their parents stay calm. A good worker owns up to errors quickly. On November 15, 2026, the top scorer owned up to cheating on a national exam with AI.

verbs.correct: To be easy to notice because it is unusual
verbs.wrong: To be written in very small letters
verbs.why: A bright red coat stands out in a crowd. A strong answer stands out on any test. The man's near-perfect results had stood out for months.

chunks.text: In a video on his lawyer's YouTube channel, he explained his [[method]]. He took photos of the questions with a tiny camera. He sent them to a generative AI tool, a program that writes answers by itself. Then he checked the answers on his smartphone. He said he {{pulled this off}} with two exam [[supervisors]] in the room. When cheating [[claims]] first {{came out}}, he [[denied]] them. He [[changed his mind]] after thinking about the person who finished second.

verbs.correct: To manage to do something hard
verbs.wrong: To delay something until a later time
verbs.why: Few students pull off a perfect score on that test. Our small team often pulls off big projects on time. He said he pulled off the cheating with two exam supervisors in the room.

verbs.correct: To become known to the public
verbs.wrong: To be counted by a machine
verbs.why: The truth often comes out in the end. News about a new phone usually comes out online first. When cheating claims first came out, the top scorer denied them.

chunks.text: He {{turned himself in}} to police in Seoul. He gave them a [[written confession]], a letter that admits what he did. He promised to {{hand over}} his [[devices]] as [[evidence]]. Police say they are {{looking into}} the case. No court has [[ruled]] on it yet. Under South Korean law, officials can {{throw out}} a cheater's results. The person is also [[banned]] from the exam for five years.

verbs.correct: To give yourself to the police
verbs.wrong: To get a job with the police
verbs.why: Some people turn themselves in because they feel guilty. A lawyer often tells a client to turn himself in. The top scorer turned himself in to police in Seoul with a written confession.

verbs.correct: To give something to another person
verbs.wrong: To fix something for another person
verbs.why: Passengers hand over their tickets at the gate. The old manager hands over the office keys to the new one. The top scorer promised to hand over his devices as evidence.

verbs.correct: To study something to learn the facts
verbs.wrong: To lock something in a police car
verbs.why: The school looks into every complaint from parents. My bank looks into strange charges on my card. Police say they are looking into the top scorer's case.

verbs.correct: To say that something does not count
verbs.wrong: To make something easier to read
verbs.why: A school throws out a test score if a student brings notes. A judge throws out evidence that police get in the wrong way. Under South Korean law, officials can throw out a cheater's results.

chunks.text: When the man confessed, South Korea's [[college entrance exam]] was {{coming up}} in four days, on Thursday, November 19, 2026. Students take this test to apply to universities. On Sunday, the president's office called an [[emergency meeting]]. A top official in the president's office said officials will {{track down}} people who cheated in the past. On Monday, November 16, the prime minister said the government will {{set up}} an emergency team. She said old ways of running exams cannot {{keep up with}} [[fast-changing]] AI.

verbs.correct: To be going to happen soon
verbs.wrong: To cost a lot of money
verbs.why: Final exams always come up fast. Tax day always comes up sooner than people expect. When the man confessed, South Korea's college entrance exam was coming up in four days.

verbs.correct: To find someone after a long search
verbs.wrong: To teach someone how to use AI
verbs.why: Police often track down car thieves in a few days. She tracks down old school friends online. A top official in the president's office said officials will track down people who cheated in the past.

verbs.wrong: To give a group a prize
verbs.why: Many cities set up special teams after a big storm. Our school sets up a group of parents to plan the summer fair. The prime minister said the government will set up an emergency team.

verbs.correct: To go at the same speed as something
verbs.wrong: To get the same grade as something
verbs.why: Laws rarely keep up with new technology. Many small schools struggle to keep up with changes in teaching. The prime minister said old ways of running exams cannot keep up with fast-changing AI.

mainIdea.s: A man who came first on a national exam for tax accountants admitted that he used AI to cheat. The case worried South Korean officials just days before the national college entrance exam.
mainIdea.why: He owned up to cheating with a tiny camera, an AI tool and a smartphone. Officials feared AI cheating because the college entrance exam was coming up.

mainIdea.s: Exam supervisors in South Korea caught a top test taker sending questions to an AI tool. Police arrested him, and leaders fear students will copy his trick at the national college test.
mainIdea.why: Close, but nobody caught him during the exam. He confessed on his own and turned himself in to police, who are looking into the case.

mainIdea.s: South Korea will let students use AI tools during its college entrance exam for the first time. Officials say the change will help students who cannot afford private tutors at home.
mainIdea.why: This story is about a top scorer who owned up to AI cheating on a tax accountant exam. The government now wants to keep the college exam fair.

lines.text: Did you hear about the exam scandal in South Korea?
The one about the tax accountant exam? I saw something about a top scorer.
Yes. On Sunday, he {{owned up to}} cheating with AI.
Wow. How did he do it?
He took photos of the questions with a tiny camera and sent them to an AI tool. Then he checked the answers on his phone.
And he {{pulled that off}} with two supervisors in the room?
Apparently. His scores {{stood out}} because he missed only one of 160 questions.
So when the cheating claims {{came out}}, people already had doubts.
Right. But at first he denied it and acted like he passed [[fair and square]].
What made him change his mind?
He said he thought about the person who finished second. Then he {{turned himself in}} to the police.
Police are {{looking into}} it. Officials can also {{throw out}} his results and ban him from the exam for five years.
He was [[playing with fire]]. A score like that was always going to get attention.
And the timing was bad. The college entrance exam was {{coming up}} that Thursday.
Are officials worried that students will try the same thing?
Very. The government will {{set up}} an emergency team, and the prime minister says old exam methods can't {{keep up with}} AI.
Cheaters always seem to be [[one step ahead]]. Still, look at him now. [[It's not worth it]].

expressions.def: Used to say that someone won or passed honestly, without cheating
ex: Our team lost, but the other team won fair and square.
She got the job fair and square.

expressions.def: Used to say that someone is doing something very risky
ex: Driving that fast on ice is playing with fire.

expressions.def: Used to say that someone is always a little faster or smarter than others
ex: Good chess players stay one step ahead.
Thieves often seem one step ahead of the police.

expressions.def: Used to say that the risk or cost is bigger than what you get
ex: You could copy his homework, but it's not worth it.
